newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US blocks Iraq oil pricing formula at UN.
newsitem.headline: US blocks Iraq oil pricing formula at UN.

text.p: The United States, as expected, has blocked the oil-pricing formula, an integral part of the oil-for-food deal between Iraq and the United Nations, U.N. officials said on Monday.
"The pricing formula has been put on hold at the request of a member state," U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said at her regular briefing. The member was identified as the United States.

The formula, which changes regularly, was last presented to the Security Council's sanctions committee in August at which time the United States also held back approval while the other 14 countries in the committee endorsed it. Another formula went to the committee last week.

Iraq officials have said that the oil-for-food plan cannot start until the pricing formula is approved. Otherwise each oil contract running through the committee would need endorsement by members rather than being approved by oil experts or overseers hired for this purpose.

The United States has said that the oil-for-food deal, which allows iraq to sell up to $2 billion of oil over six months to pay for food, medicine and other necessities for its people, is on hold for other reasons and Iraq's accusations are out of line.

The plan was about to be implemented in September when Iraq sent troops into the northern Kurdish province to aid one of the warring factions. The United Nations suspended implementing the plan because of the security threat.

Since then Iraq has demanded replacing local staff members the U.N. had hired, cutting its 150-person monitoring staff in half, curtailing monitors' freedom of movement and making Baghdad the benficiary of a U.N. escrow account set up to receive oil revenues.

But Iraqi envoys say these obstacles could be solved if the pricing formula were enacted. U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright said earlier this month that Washington would approve the formula once Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali decided the deal could go ahead.
Nevertheless, some diplomats on the committee believe that U.S. hesitancy on the formula is a political move to give Washington more control over the plan.
